```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(scales)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(httpgd)

# set plot theme
theme_set(theme_bw())
```

# Load and preview data

Read data from the `ratings.csv` file
```{r load-data}
ratings <- read_csv('ratings.csv',
                    col_names = c('user_id','movie_id','rating','timestamp'))
```

Loaded `r format(object.size(ratings), units="Mb")` of ratings data, containing `r format(nrow(ratings), big.mark = ",")` ratings. Here's a preview:
```{r preview-data}
head(ratings) %>% kable()
```

# Summary statistics

```{r dist-ratings}
# plot the distribution of rating values https://speakerdeck.com/jhofman/modeling-social-data-lecture-2-introduction-to-counting?slide=26
ratings %>%
  group_by(rating) %>%  
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x=rating)) +
  scale_y_continuous(label = comma) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = "white", fill = "pink") +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Review Count (Watches)", title = "Distribution of Rating Values")
```

## Per-movie stats

```{r aggregate-by-movie}
# aggregate ratings by movie, computing mean rating and number of ratings
# hint: use the n() function for easy counting within a group
ratings_by_movie <- ratings %>%
  group_by(movie_id) %>%
  summarize(count = n(), mean = mean(rating)) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))
```

```{r dist-movie-popularity}
# plot distribution of movie popularity (= number of ratings the movie received)
# hint: try scale_x_log10() for a logarithmic x axis
ggplot(ratings_by_movie, aes(x = count)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "pink") +
  scale_x_log10(label = comma) +
  labs(x = "Number of Movie Ratings", y = "Number of Movies", title = "Distribution of Movie Popularity")
```

```{r dist-mean-ratings-by-movie}
# plot distribution of mean ratings by movie https://speakerdeck.com/jhofman/modeling-social-data-lecture-2-introduction-to-counting?slide=28
# hint: try geom_histogram and geom_density
ggplot(ratings_by_movie, aes(x = mean)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "pink") +
  labs(x = "Mean Rating by Movie", y = "Density", title = "Distribution of Mean Ratings by Movie")

ggplot(ratings_by_movie, aes(x = mean)) +
  geom_density(fill = 'pink') +
  labs(x = "Mean Rating by Movie", y = "Density", title = "Distribution of Mean Ratings by Movie")
```

```{r cdf-movie-pop}
# rank movies by popularity (number of ratings) and compute the cdf, or fraction of all views covered by the top-k movies https://speakerdeck.com/jhofman/modeling-social-data-lecture-2-introduction-to-counting?slide=30
# hint: use dplyr's rank and arrange functions, and the base R sum and cumsum functions
# store the result in a new data frame so you can use it in creating figure 2 from the paper below
by_popularity <- ratings %>%
  group_by(movie_id) %>%
  summarize(count = n(), mean = mean(rating)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(count)) %>% 
  mutate(rank = rank(row_number()), all_movies = sum(count), cum_movies = cumsum(count), cdf = cum_movies / all_movies)
by_popularity
# plot the CDF of movie popularity
ggplot(by_popularity, aes(x = rank, y = cdf)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(label = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Movie Rank", y = "CDF (Percent)", title = "Fraction of all views covered")
```


# Per-user stats

```{r aggregate-by-user}
# aggregate ratings by user, computing mean and number of ratings
ratings_by_user <- ratings %>% 
  group_by(user_id) %>% 
  summarize(num_of_ratings = n(), mean_rating = mean(rating))
```

```{r dist-user-activity}
# plot distribution of user activity (= number of ratings the user made)
# hint: try a log scale here
ggplot(ratings_by_user, aes(x = num_of_ratings)) +
  scale_x_log10(label = comma) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "pink") +
  labs(x = "Number of Ratings", y = "Number of Users", title = "User Activity (Num of Users vs Num of Ratings)")
```

# Anatomy of the long tail

```{r long-tail}
# generate the equivalent of figure 2a of this paper:
# note: don't worry about the "null model" lines
# just do the solid lines and dotted line (optional)
# https://5harad.com/papers/long_tail.pdf

# Specifically, for the subset of users who rated at least 10 movies,
# produce a plot that shows the fraction of users satisfied (vertical
# axis) as a function of inventory size (horizontal axis). We will
# define "satisfied" as follows: an individual user is satisfied p% of
# the time at inventory of size k if at least p% of the movies they
# rated are contained in the top k most popular movies. As in the
# paper, produce one curve for the 100% user satisfaction level and
# another for 90%---do not, however, bother implementing the null
# model (shown in the dashed lines).

# inventory size (list of movies in order of rank) 
# x = rank
# user satisfaction (point at which least popular movie reviwed is considered)

# for each user, I want to see their most niche movie review
# by_popularity has each movies rank
user_satisfaction <- ratings_by_user %>% 
  filter(num_of_ratings >= 10) %>% 
  select(user_id, num_of_ratings) %>%
  mutate(ninety_satisfaction = trunc((num_of_ratings) * .90), full_satisfaction = num_of_ratings)

longtail_data <- by_popularity %>% 
  select(movie_id, count, rank) %>% # grabbing impt values
  left_join(ratings, by = "movie_id") %>% # to connect user_id to movie_id (users to movies they reviewed)
  select(movie_id, count, rank, user_id) %>% # grabbing impt values
  left_join(user_satisfaction, by = "user_id") %>% # to add each users number of ratings, satisfaction rank
  select(movie_id, rank, user_id, ninety_satisfaction, full_satisfaction) %>% 
  ## At this point I have all the values I want in the data frame
  pivot_longer(`ninety_satisfaction`:`full_satisfaction`, names_to = "satisfaction_level", values_to = "needed_review_rank") %>%
  ## I do the above to make satisfaction level a column i can group by so i can have two lines
  group_by(user_id, satisfaction_level) %>% # grouping by user so i can isolate the highest ranked movie to reach the satisfaction level
  arrange(user_id, rank) %>% # arranging by rank so I can grab by row num (kth )
  filter(row_number() == needed_review_rank) %>% # for each user and satisfaction level filter out only the row that matches the neededrank
  group_by(rank, satisfaction_level) %>%
  summarize(count = n()) %>% # counts the number of users that would be satisfied
  group_by(satisfaction_level) %>%  
  arrange(rank) %>%
  mutate(total_users = sum(count), cum_users = cumsum(count), satisfaction = cum_users/total_users) 

ggplot(longtail_data, aes(x = rank, y = satisfaction, group = satisfaction_level)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3000, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Inventory Size", y = "Percent of Users Satisfied", title = "90 and 100 Percent Satisfaction Levels")
 
```
